Jehoash (Joash) of Israel
jeh-HO-ash (or JOH-ash)
proper noun (figure)
Hebrew Yehoash / Yoash (H3060 / H3101) — "Yahweh has bestowed" or "Yahweh-given." The longer and shorter forms refer to the same name; the same name was simultaneously borne by Joash of Judah (the eighth king of the southern kingdom, hidden in the temple by his aunt Jehosheba).

📖 Biblical Definition

Jehoash of Israel (c. 798 — 782 BC), also called Joash, was the twelfth king of the divided northern kingdom (2 Kings 13:10-25; 2 Kings 14:8-16), son of Jehoahaz, third king of the Jehu dynasty, who reigned sixteen years and recovered the Israelite cities Hazael of Aram had taken from his father. His reign overlapped the final years of the prophet Elisha; the dying Elisha summoned him for the famous bow-and-arrows episode (2 Kings 13:14-19), in which Elisha had Joash shoot an arrow eastward (the 'arrow of the LORD's deliverance from Syria') and then strike the ground with the remaining arrows; Joash struck only three times and stopped, and Elisha grieved that he had not struck five or six times because his victory over Aram would now be limited to three. The prophecy was precisely fulfilled: Joash defeated Hazael's son Ben-Hadad three times and recovered the cities. Joash also captured King Amaziah of Judah at Beth-shemesh after Amaziah's pride-driven challenge, broke down four hundred cubits of Jerusalem's wall, and carried the temple treasures to Samaria (2 Chr 25:23-24).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Twelfth king of Israel (c. 798-782 BC); son of Jehoahaz; reigned 16 years; recovered Israelite cities from Aram; received the bow-and-arrows prophecy from the dying Elisha (2 Kings 13:14-19); captured Amaziah of Judah at Beth-shemesh.

JEHOASH (JOASH) OF ISRAEL, proper noun. Hebrew Yehoash / Yoash (H3060 / H3101) — "Yahweh has bestowed."

Twelfth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (c. 798-782 BC); son of Jehoahaz; third king of the Jehu dynasty.

16-year reign; recovered cities Hazael had taken from his father; defeated Aram three times under the dying Elisha's bow-and-arrows prophecy.

Captured King Amaziah of Judah at Beth-shemesh; broke down 400 cubits of Jerusalem's wall; carried temple treasures to Samaria.

Distinct from Joash king of Judah (his contemporary; the boy-king hidden in the temple by Jehosheba).

📖 Key Scripture

2 Kings 13:14-17 — "Now Elisha was fallen sick of his sickness whereof he died. And Joash the king of Israel came down unto him, and wept over his face... And Elisha said unto him, Take bow and arrows. And he took unto him bow and arrows. And he said to the king of Israel, Put thine hand upon the bow. And he put his hand upon it: and Elisha put his hands upon the king's hands. And he said, Open the window eastward... And he said, The arrow of the LORD's deliverance, and the arrow of deliverance from Syria."

2 Kings 13:18-19 — "And he said, Take the arrows. And he took them. And he said unto the king of Israel, Smite upon the ground. And he smote thrice, and stayed. And the man of God was wroth with him, and said, Thou shouldest have smitten five or six times; then hadst thou smitten Syria till thou hadst consumed it: whereas now thou shalt smite Syria but thrice."

2 Kings 14:11-12 — "But Amaziah would not hear. Therefore Jehoash king of Israel went up; and he and Amaziah king of Judah looked one another in the face at Beth-shemesh, which belongeth to Judah. And Judah was put to the worse before Israel; and they fled every man to their tents."

2 Kings 14:13-14 — "And Jehoash king of Israel took Amaziah king of Judah... at Beth-shemesh, and came to Jerusalem, and brake down the wall of Jerusalem from the gate of Ephraim unto the corner gate, four hundred cubits. And he took all the gold and silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of the LORD, and in the treasures of the king's house..."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Jehoash of Israel is corrupted when he is confused with Joash of Judah (his exact contemporary with the same name in the rival kingdom), when the bow-and-arrows prophecy is read as merely picturesque rather than as a prophetic-conditional teaching on the relation between obedience and victory, or when his sack of Jerusalem is treated as merely military success rather than as covenant judgment on Amaziah's pride.

expand to see more

Two simultaneous Joashes. The Hebrew name Joash/Jehoash was simultaneously borne by the 8th king of Judah (the boy-king hidden by Jehosheba; 2 Kings 11-12) and the 12th king of Israel (this one). Modern readers sometimes confuse them. The narrator distinguishes carefully: Joash of Judah was a Davidic king of the southern kingdom; Jehoash of Israel was a Jehu-dynasty king of the northern kingdom; their reigns overlapped and they fought each other in person at Beth-shemesh (Jehoash captured and humiliated his Judean namesake's son Amaziah). Two kings; one name; opposite kingdoms.

Bow-and-arrows as picturesque. The dying Elisha's bow-and-arrows scene (2 Kings 13:14-19) is sometimes read as colorful prophet-theater. The chapter is teaching a serious doctrine: prophetic promise is conditional on the persistence and faith of those receiving it. Joash stopped striking the ground after three blows because he did not press in fully; the prophet's grief was theological. Half-hearted reception of God's offered grace produces half-hearted realization of God's offered deliverance. The same principle frames Matthew 13:58 ('he did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief').
